findings.description: The policy grants ec2:*, s3:*, lambda:*, and cloudwatch:* on Resource "*", giving this single user full control over compute, storage, serverless, and monitoring services including the ability to read/exfiltrate all S3 objects, modify or delete EC2 instances, and disable logging. This is far beyond what a deploy identity needs and constitutes a privilege-escalation and full-account-compromise path if the access key leaks.

Combined with the wildcard actions, "Resource": "*" means there is no resource-level restriction, so the credentials can act on every S3 bucket, EC2 instance, and Lambda function in the account, including any created by other teams or environments.

A static IAM access key is created for the deployment user with no rotation. Long-lived keys cannot be scoped to short sessions and, combined with the wildcard admin-like policy, create a standing credential that grants full control of the account if exposed.

The access key is emitted as a Terraform output, so the credential material is written to state and printed in plan/apply logs and CI output. It is not marked sensitive = true, so it is displayed in plaintext to anyone with access to the console or logs.

A long-lived IAM user with force_destroy = true is used for deployment rather than an assumable role with temporary credentials; force_destroy also removes the user (and allows its keys/policies to be destroyed) without protection, weakening credential hygiene and the audit trail.
